meta: Jusepe de Ribera's 1632 painting of Ixion, bound in chains and tortured by Zeus, one of a series of four condemned figures.
about: Chains bind a muscular nude man whose body twists and shortens sharply against a dark ground. He is Ixion, whom Zeus punished with eternal torture in Greek myth. Jusepe de Ribera signed and dated the painting in 1632. It was one of a series of four paintings of the condemned, the others showing Sisyphus and Tantalus. The Prado holds Ixion and the Tityos. Sisyphus and Tantalus are lost.

meta: Murillo's Aranjuez Immaculate Conception, painted around 1675 and named after the palace chapel where it was first recorded.
about: A woman in a white robe and blue mantle rises on clouds, her hands crossed over her chest and her eyes lifted. Putti gather at the base of the canvas. Bartolomé Esteban Murillo painted her around 1675. The picture takes its name from the palace at Aranjuez, where it first turns up in written records in 1818. It hung in the royal chapel of San Antonio. By 1827 it was in the queen's quarters of the same palace. It is now in the Prado.

meta: Peter Paul Rubens's The Origin of the Milky Way, painted for Philip IV's hunting lodge, shows Hera spilling her milk across the sky.
about: Milk arcs across a dark, star-filled sky from the breast of a nude goddess beside a chariot drawn by peacocks. Peter Paul Rubens painted this scene of Hera, known to the Romans as Juno, spilling her milk over the infant Heracles. Zeus looks on, identifiable by his eagle. Hera's face is modelled on Rubens's wife, Hélène Fourment. Philip IV of Spain commissioned it for the Torre de la Parada, his hunting lodge near Madrid, as one of 112 paintings based on Ovid. It is now in the Prado.

meta: David Teniers the Younger's 1665 peasant kermis: dancing outside an inn, a drunk man among the pigs and a banner in the window.
about: Outside an inn, peasants dance to a bagpiper while large parties eat and drink at long tables on either side. A drunk man has fallen among the pigs, and his wife is hauling him back to his feet. At left a maid draws water from a well. A banner showing a knight with a bow and arrows hangs from the inn window. David Teniers the Younger signed the picture on a block of stone at lower right. The city of Amsterdam lent it to the Rijksmuseum from the A. van der Hoop bequest.

meta: Johan Diderik Cornelis Veltens's 1865 drawing of the surroundings of the Polderhuis, kept in the Atlas Van Eck.
about: A canal runs between wooden houses, past a tall chimney and a sluice or mill with paddle wheels on the right. Small rowing boats and figures move along the water, and a woman with laundry stands on the bank beside a dog. Johan Diderik Cornelis Veltens drew the scene in pencil, pen and brush in grey. It belongs to the Atlas Van Eck, where the drawings are sorted by district number, and this one is filed under 26. The Koninklijk Oudheidkundig Genootschap lends it to the Rijksmuseum.

meta: Albrecht Dürer's 1510 woodcut of Veronica holding the sweat cloth with the face of Christ, from the Small Passion series.
about: Veronica holds up the sweat cloth bearing the face of Christ, with Saint Peter and Saint Paul standing on either side. Peter has his keys and Paul his sword. Albrecht Dürer made this woodcut in 1510. It belongs to the Small Passion, a series of a title print and 36 scenes from the Bible, most of them from the story of Christ's suffering. The face on the cloth wears a crown of thorns.

meta: Gerbrand van den Eeckhout's 1663 watercolour view of Rhenen and the Rhine, bought by the Rijksmuseum in 1894.
about: A broad river landscape opens out beneath the church tower of Rhenen, which rises above the houses of a town on a low ridge. Small sailing boats sit on the water at left. Gerbrand van den Eeckhout drew it in 1663 in watercolour over black chalk and graphite. The drawing was sold at an Amsterdam sale in 1893, and the next year the Rijksmuseum bought it from the dealer H.J. Valk for 22 guilders 95.

meta: Gerbrand van den Eeckhout's 1667 pen drawing of guild officers around a table, sold in 1847 as a sketch for a painting.
about: Men in wide-brimmed hats and lace collars gather around a table, some seated and one standing behind them. Gerbrand van den Eeckhout drew them in 1667 with pen and brown ink in loose, quick strokes. An 1847 sale catalogue described the sheet as a sketch for a painting that had belonged to the guild of gaugers in Amsterdam. The Rijksmuseum bought it with support from the Vereniging Rembrandt.

meta: Gerbrand van den Eeckhout's 1653 chalk drawing of a boy asleep in a chair, with a collecting history back to 1800.
about: A boy in a wide-brimmed hat and buttoned jacket sleeps slumped sideways in a wooden chair. Gerbrand van den Eeckhout drew him in black chalk with grey wash. The sheet belonged to the collector Cornelis Ploos van Amstel, whose sale in 1800 listed it as a young man asleep on a chair. It went in a lot with two other drawings for 5 guilders 50. In 1871 it was sold again in Rotterdam from the collection of Dirk Vis Blokhuyzen and bought for 1 guilder by Baron Willem van Reede van Oudtshoorn.

meta: Samuel Bottschild's 1693 etching of Nox, Night, from a series of 48 prints mostly designed for ceilings.
about: A winged woman holds a crescent moon and scatters stars, while a figure sleeps beside her at lower right. The word Nox is inscribed at the foot of the circle. Samuel Bottschild etched it for a series published in 1693, Opera Varia Historica, Poetica & Iconologica. The series has 48 prints and covers almost everything the artist made. Most of them are designs for ceilings.

meta: Christoffel van Sichem the Younger's 1629 woodcut of the Tree of Jesse, first used in the book Der Zielen Lust-hof.
about: Jesse lies at the bottom with his elbow on a stone, and a tree grows from his body. The ancestors of Christ sit on its branches, and the Virgin with the Child crowns the top. Christoffel van Sichem the Younger made the woodcut, which came from the publisher P.J. Paets in Amsterdam. It was first used in the book Der Zielen Lust-hof, printed in Leuven for Paets in 1629. The museum's copy is mounted on an album sheet.

meta: Romeyn de Hooghe's 1690 bird's-eye print of Het Loo Palace, part of a much larger view with thirteen smaller scenes around it.
about: A bird's-eye view takes in a palace and its formal gardens, with geometric parterres, rows of clipped trees and fountains. Carriages and horsemen move through the grounds. Romeyn de Hooghe made the print in 1690, but it is only part of a bigger work. The museum describes it as half of a view of Het Loo, spread over four sheets or possibly two. The whole print put the palace in the middle, with thirteen views of its buildings and park around it and a profile of the palace at the bottom.

meta: Charles Emile Jacque's 1864 etching of a path, a cow and a seated woman with a child, from a series of 25 rural scenes.
about: A dirt path winds through open ground between a tall poplar and a broad leafy tree. In the foreground a woman sits beside a small child holding a stick, and a cow grazes nearby. Charles Emile Jacque etched it in 1864. It comes from an untitled series of 25 prints with rural and pastoral subjects, which was published that year.

meta: Jan Brandes's 1778 watercolour of a Cape chestnut branch in flower, drawn at the Constantia estate near the Cape of Good Hope.
about: A branch of broad green leaves and pink star-shaped flowers fills the sheet, with a small sketch below it. Jan Brandes drew it on 23 October 1778 at Constantia, an estate at the Cape of Good Hope. He had asked its owner, Mr Leseur, to have a twig cut so that he could take a look. The tree was only just beginning to flower and leaf. Brandes wrote that the fruit would be like a cherry with a small seed, which chickens and turkeys ate as soon as it fell. Nobody knew the name. The drawing comes from the first volume of his sketchbook.

meta: John Raphael Smith's 1780 mezzotint The Fruit-Barrow, after H. Walton, a group portrait of uncertain identity.
about: A fruit seller stands at a barrow beside a brick wall with ivy, attended by a woman in a long gown and feathered hat and several children. The mezzotint is titled The Fruit-Barrow. It was painted by H. Walton and engraved by John Raphael Smith around 1780. Nobody is sure who the family is. The Rijksmuseum suggests it may be a Mrs Carr, or else members of the family of Henry Walton.

meta: Daniël Bruyninx's signed 1761 miniature portrait of a man in a blue coat, set in a silver case.
about: A man with powdered grey hair wears a blue coat with gold embroidered trim over a red waistcoat and a black neckcloth. The portrait is a small oval miniature set in an open silver case lined with green velvet. Daniël Bruyninx signed and dated it 1761. In 1918 a dealer named Van Waegeningh in The Hague sold it for 125 guilders to Adolph Staring van de Wildenborch of Deventer. His widow later gave it to the museum, with other objects, in 1981.

meta: Jan van Noordt's 1664 portrait of the Amsterdam merchant Dionijs Wijnands, shown to the knees beside a table with his hat and gloves.
about: A man stands at a table, shown to the knees, with his hat and gloves lying on the tabletop. He wears black with a broad white collar and gold-trimmed cuffs, and an arched opening at the right looks out on a stormy sky. Jan van Noordt signed the portrait in 1664. The sitter is Dionijs Wijnands, an Amsterdam merchant who lived from 1628 to 1673. He was the son of Hendrick Wijnands and Aeltje Denijs. The portrait reached the Rijksmuseum in the bequest of Jonkheer J.S.H. van de Poll.

meta: Joseph Boze's signed miniature portrait of Gerrit Jan van Houten, later burgomaster of Amersfoort, painted around 1790.
about: A smiling man with curly dark hair wears a dark high-collared coat and a white frilled cravat against a pale grey-blue ground. Joseph Boze painted this oval miniature around 1790 and signed it. The sitter is Gerrit Jan van Houten, who became burgomaster of Amersfoort. It has a pendant in the same museum. Lieutenant-Colonel Marius Cornelis van Houten gave it to the Rijksmuseum in 1933 but kept the use of it for life. It passed to the museum in 1953.
